pages.text: Terrier Group · Northumberland, England BedlingtonTerrier A lamb's coat over a lion's heart. It looks like something that wandered out of a flock — curly, pale, and softly arched. Then it moves, and the disguise falls apart. Underneath that woolly coat is a fast, wiry, unbelievably game little dog bred by coal miners to kill vermin and keep up with a poacher on the run. The coat is the whole illusion — crisp, curling, and quietly ridiculous. Height 15–17.5 in38–44 cm Weight 17–23 lb7.7–10.4 kg Lifespan 11–16 years AKC recognised 1886 01 Origins The breed takes its name from Bedlington, a mining town in Northumberland in the north-east of England. Before that it was called the Rothbury Terrier, after the nearby village where the type was concentrated in the early 1800s; a mason there named Joseph Aynsley was the first to call his dogs Bedlingtons, in 1825. Its job description was blunt: kill rats in the pits, work badger and fox above ground, and run down a rabbit for the pot. It kept the company of miners and poachers rather than gentlemen, which is exactly why it was built for speed as much as grit — a dog that had to catch dinner and then leave the field quickly. Whippet is generally credited for the turn of speed, Otterhound for the love of water. ◎ Bedlington, Northumberland — 55.131° N, 1.593° W openstreetmap.org · loads on click Ten miles north of Newcastle upon Tyne. Open the full map. 02 The look Nothing about the silhouette is accidental. The head is a narrow pear — wedge-shaped, rounded at the skull, with no stop at all, so the profile runs in one unbroken line from crown to nose. The ears hang flat and finish in a small tassel of fine hair. The back arches over the loin and the tuck-up is deep, giving the same lines you see in a sighthound. That is a galloping frame wearing a terrier's coat. The coat itself is the give-away: a crisp mixture of hard and soft hair that stands off the body and curls, especially on the head and face. It sheds very little. Colours are blue, liver, and sandy, each also seen with tan markings. Puppies are born dark and lighten as they mature — a blue puppy arrives nearly black. The numbers page has the standard's ranges drawn out. 03 Temperament Indoors, a Bedlington is a mild, affectionate, slightly theatrical companion that would rather be touching you than not. They are quieter in the house than most terriers and attach themselves hard to their people. Outdoors is a different animal. The prey drive is genuine and the acceleration is real, so a reliable recall and a secure fence matter more here than with a comparably sized companion breed. They are game rather than quarrelsome — slow to start something, but historically not built to back down from it either. 04 Living with one The coat does not shed itself, which means you deal with it instead: clipping and tidying roughly every six to eight weeks, plus regular brushing between visits. In exchange you get a dog that leaves very little hair on the sofa. There is a longer piece on the coat in the journal. Exercise needs are about intensity, not duration. A Bedlington that gets to sprint is satisfied; one taken on nothing but slow leash walks generally is not. One health note worth knowing The breed carries an inherited copper storage disorder — copper toxicosis — in which copper accumulates in the liver instead of being cleared. It is linked to the COMMD1 gene and a DNA test exists, so responsible breeders screen for it. If you are looking at a puppy, ask about the parents' copper testing — how to read the results. 05 See one in motion Two introductions, one in English and one in Chinese. Neither loads until you click — the page itself asks nothing of YouTube or Bilibili until you do. ▶ Bedlington Terrier — AKC Dog Breed Series youtube.com · loads on click American Kennel Club, 2015. pages.text: 10 August 2026 · 4 min read · Journal The coat is the whole job Most breed pages file grooming under "care", somewhere below diet. For a Bedlington it belongs at the top, because the coat is not a maintenance detail — it is the single biggest practical difference between this dog and a similarly sized companion breed. Why it does not shed The Bedlington coat is a crisp mixture of hard and soft hair that stands away from the body and curls, most tightly on the head and face. Hairs that would otherwise be dropped stay caught in that curl. The upside is real and it is the reason many people choose the breed: very little hair on the sofa, on your clothes, or in the car. The downside is the exact same fact stated differently. Hair that does not fall out has to be removed by someone, on a schedule, forever. A low-shedding coat is not a low-maintenance coat. It is a coat whose maintenance has been moved from your vacuum cleaner to your calendar. What the schedule actually looks like Every six to eight weeks: a full clip. Left longer than that, the curl starts to mat close to the skin, and matting is not something brushing fixes after the fact. Weekly, or better: brushing through, with particular attention behind the ears, in the armpits, and around the harness line, which are the three places mats form first. Between clips: tidying the face furnishings and the feet, which grow at an inconvenient rate. Either you learn to do this with clippers at home, or you budget for a groomer eight or nine times a year. Both are legitimate; neither is optional. The dog in the photograph on the front page is about four weeks past a clip, which is why the face looks like a cloud. The show trim, and why it looks like that The outline you see in the ring — narrow pear-shaped head, tasselled ear tips, arched loin, tight tuck-up — is partly the dog and partly the scissoring. The trim exaggerates a shape that is genuinely there. Underneath it is a galloping frame with a terrier's temperament, and the clip is drawing your eye to that arch on purpose. A pet clip does not need to reproduce any of this. Shorter all over is easier to keep, more comfortable in summer, and grows back into the same dog. The only thing that matters at home is that it does not mat. The numbers page has the standard's colour list — blue, liver, sandy, each with or without tan — and one detail worth knowing before you pick a puppy on colour: they all arrive much darker than they end up.

pages.text: 3 August 2026 · 5 min read · Journal Copper testing, explained plainly If you ask a Bedlington breeder exactly one health question, make it this one. The breed is closely associated with an inherited copper storage disorder, and it is the rare case where a cheap cheek swab tells you something genuinely useful before you commit to a dog for the next fourteen years. What the disease is Healthy livers excrete surplus copper in bile. In affected Bedlingtons that clearance is impaired, so dietary copper accumulates in liver tissue over years. Enough accumulation damages the liver. It is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, which is the technical way of saying a dog needs two copies of the faulty version — one from each parent — to be affected, and that two apparently healthy parents can produce an affected puppy. In most affected Bedlingtons the cause is a deletion in the COMMD1 gene (older papers call it MURR1). That is what the commercial DNA test looks for. The three results, and what each one means Clear — two normal copies. The dog will not develop the COMMD1 form of the disease and cannot pass a faulty copy on. Carrier — one normal, one faulty. The dog itself is not expected to be affected, but half its puppies inherit the faulty copy on average. A carrier bred to a clear dog produces no affected puppies. Affected — two faulty copies. At risk of copper accumulation, and every one of its puppies inherits at least one faulty copy. This is why "both parents tested clear" is a much stronger answer than "the puppies look fine". Under recessive inheritance, health you can see tells you very little about what a dog carries. The caveat that matters A clear DNA test lowers the risk considerably. It does not reduce it to zero. Copper accumulation has been reported in Bedlingtons that do not carry the COMMD1 deletion, so the test cannot be read as a guarantee against liver disease in general — only against that specific known variant. The definitive assessment of how much copper is actually in a liver is a biopsy with quantitative copper measurement, which is a veterinary decision and not something a puppy buyer arranges on a hunch. Practically, that means the DNA result belongs in the same mental bucket as the rest of a breeder's paperwork: strong evidence, not a warranty. What to actually ask Have both parents been DNA tested for the COMMD1 variant, and can I see the certificates? What were the results — clear, carrier, or affected? If either parent is a carrier, what was the other parent's result? Has any dog in the line been diagnosed with liver disease, and at what age? A breeder who welcomes these questions is the answer to several other questions you have not thought to ask yet. One who is vague about paperwork is also answering something. This is a plain-language summary for prospective owners, not veterinary advice. Diagnosis, testing and treatment decisions belong with your vet. Sources are listed on the numbers page.
